Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
Dorothea is an 80-year-old woman of European descent who has worked as a social worker for most of her adult life, spending decades advocating for vulnerable clients in crisis - people whose suffering she understood, she once thought, because she had been spared it herself. She presents now as a single woman living alone, referred through her own agency's employee assistance programme after a colleague noticed she had begun refusing to conduct home visits and had stopped attending team meetings held in small conference rooms. She is soft-spoken in session, precise with language in the way that long professional training produces, and visibly startled by any sound from the corridor outside the office.

The abuse took place over approximately three years with a man she had been involved with since her late seventies, a widower she had met through a mutual friend. The relationship began warmly, and Dorothea had permitted herself, after decades of independence, to believe that companionship at this stage of life was both possible and safe. The violence escalated gradually. What she returns to most often - and what she returns to involuntarily, in fragments she cannot fully assemble - are several specific moments: the sound of his key turning in the lock, or the door being thrown open, which meant that what followed would be bad; the sight of his face across a small room; the feeling of being unable to move toward an exit. She cannot reconstruct the sequence of events across those years into a coherent story. What she has instead are discrete images, each one vivid and still: his shadow in a doorway, the pattern of a rug she stared at, the particular quality of afternoon light on a certain day. When these images surface, what overtakes her is not fear alone but something she describes as grief so total it feels physical - a mourning she cannot name the object of, though the therapist understands it as the loss of the self she had been before.

In the months since leaving the relationship, Dorothea has reorganised her life around a set of quiet but far-reaching adjustments. She no longer works with male clients and has constructed a plausible professional rationale for this that has so far gone unchallenged. When she enters any room - the office kitchen, a waiting area, a community centre where she facilitates a support group for elderly women - she locates the exits before she does anything else, her eyes moving to the doors before she has consciously decided to look. She does not sleep well. She lies awake for long stretches, and on the nights when she has learned that sleep is more likely to bring disturbance, she keeps a lamp on and reads until nearly dawn, accepting exhaustion as the lesser cost. She has also, in ways she finds difficult to articulate, tried simply not to think about what happened - to press the memories down and away - though she acknowledges this has not worked and that the images return regardless.

What has perhaps changed most visibly is her relationship to the professional identity she spent her life building. Dorothea has always understood people, has always believed, in some foundational way, that human beings are essentially knowable and that the world, while imperfect, operates according to principles she could navigate. She had come to believe none of that was true anymore. People, she now felt with quiet certainty, could not be trusted - a conviction that sat uneasily against fifty years of social work practice and that she had not yet spoken aloud to anyone before these sessions. She also carries something she calls a feeling of being soiled, a sense she cannot fully rationalise but cannot dismiss, that what was done to her has left a mark on her that others, if they looked carefully, might see.

She has also spent considerable time asking why this happened to her, turning the question over without resolution, as though the right answer might restore something. She came to seek help not after any single crisis but after realising, during a supervision session with a young colleague, that she could not be alone in a room with that colleague's male supervisor without her heart hammering and her attention fixed on the door. What she most hopes for, she says carefully, is to be able to do her work again. What she most fears is that the person who could do that work no longer exists.
